Hello, all. I just finished Mawaru Penguindrum tonight and would like to share my thoughts on it, and possibly discuss with others who've seen the shows. As with all of Ikuhara's other works (Utena and Yuri Kuma), Penguindrum is rife with symbolism. I'm not nearly intelligent enough to break down every single part of this show, but I feel that I have a pretty good handle on the major themes. Would love to hear everyone else's thoughts.

Be warned: There will be spoilers beneath the line below. If you have not seen Penguindrum, but want a spoiler-free recommendation of it, wait a day or so and I'll have one of those up.

BEWARE: Major spoilers for Mawaru Penguindrum ahead.

Without further ado, I'm going to jump right into it:

Kanba, Shouma, and Himari are all the children of the Takakuras, although Shouma is the only blood child. This is because they all share a bond as “family”, and because of this bond, they share a fate. In essence, when one person forms a bond with another, they become incorporated into each others' fates, whether that be good or bad. In the case of the Takakura children, Kanba and Himari took on the curse placed upon Shouma's family because of the sins that they had committed. The sin was that of trying to change the status quo, or revolutionize the world (a theme explored in Shoujo Kakumei Utena). In other words, the Kiga Group was trying to change their own fate because the current world order benefited the greedy, and they wanted a more egalitarian world. Altering the path of one's fate comes at a heavy price, and the Kiga Group was ready to sacrifice many innocents to do so (which is a sort of greedy thing to do, anyway). Sanetoshi is the embodiment of the curse that is the price of revolution. Momoka, on the other hand, is a symbol of accepting one's fate because it is not just to sacrifice others for one's own gain. Ironically, Momoka does this by incurring the price of change upon herself. She accepts others' fates onto herself, which ultimately leads to her death. Her death also illustrates how bonds intertwine people's fates, as Tabuki, Yuri, and Ringo were all deeply affected by Momoka's passing. However, all of those close to Momoka did not realize that she was taking the price of fate onto herself, and ended up blaming the Takakuras for her death (minus Ringo), or trying to take her place.

Coming back to the Takakuras, the children ended up inheriting their parents' crimes, yet Himari was the only one that suffered for it, symbolized by her illness. Kanba and Shouma adored their sister and wanted to protect her. Kanba sought to achieve this by taking on the role of the Takakura parents and leading the Kiga Group to change the world. Shouma, on the other hand, wanted to leave behind his family's past, and save Himari by divorcing the Takakura family from the crimes of the Kiga Group. In the end, neither of these things worked. In Kanba's case, repeating the crimes of the past would only lead to more ill will against the family. In Shouma's case, it is impossible to leave behind the legacy of one's parents because the effect that parents have on their children is integral to said children's selves. We see how children are affected by their parents several times throughout the series:

  • Shouma, Kanba, and Himari bear the curse of the Kiga Group's actions

  • Ringo feels the need to become Momoka because of her mother's mourning

  • Tabuki feels unneeded by his mother, and almost becomes and invisible entity

  • Yuri is abused by her father, and becomes incapable of relating to others

  • Mario was influenced by his grandfather, and nearly became a similar person

This is another facet of the fate that one's parents pass down to him/her. The person one is affects where one ends up, and if someone grows up in a broken situation, they end up a broken person. So, not only must people pay for the sins that their parents commit against others, but they are also affected by the sins they commit against them.

Finally, Kanba and Shouma realize that they are inseparable from the sins of their parents and the fates that they have incurred. Although Kanba is not Shouma's blood brothers, they are brothers in fate because they are both tied to the Kiga Group's activities (Kanba's actual father was a member of the Group). In this way, they share a fate, as represented by the apple (or fruit of fate) that they shared when they were trapped within themselves (which is a whole other line of symbolism to be examined). However, the people that they loved (Himari and Ringo) were also drawn into their fate through their bonds. In a grand paradox, Kanba and Shouma realize that loving someone means not wanting them to come to harm. However, the very fact that they are attached to others means that these others will come to harm because, by forming bonds, they partake in each others' fates. Thus, the only solution is to take the punishment for their parent's crimes and erase themselves from the lives of Himari and Ringo. Again, we are confronted with a paradox in which, in order to protect the ones that they love, Kanba and Shouma have to delete all of the memories that they have with these people, or, in other words, they have to destroy the reason that they love them, in the first place. So, Mawaru Penguindrum is about the paradoxical nature of bonds. The bonds one has with their parents affect them and these effects are mirrored in their relationships with others. These bonds can be harmful to loved ones, yet without these bonds they cannot be loved ones. Which is better: To have a relationship, but hurt the other, or never have the relationship and never harm the other?
